JAMES CADDELL IN HIS OWN VOICE: "TRAVELING OUT OF THE COMFORT ZONE"
McGill News (alumni quarterly), Fall 2004, in two pages.
Recovered 2026-09-07.

=====================================================================
WHY IT WAS "DEAD", AND IT WAS NOT
=====================================================================

This project's source record src_mcgill_news_caddell carried the URL

    .../news-archives/2004/fall/travelin

and a read state of "asserted:fetched-page1-page2-404". THE URL IS TRUNCATED BY
TWO CHARACTERS AND A PATH SEGMENT. The article is at

    https://mcgillnews-archives.mcgill.ca/news-archives/2004/fall/traveling/index.html
    https://mcgillnews-archives.mcgill.ca/news-archives/2004/fall/traveling/two/index.html

Both return HTTP 200 today with a browser user-agent. The 404 was a fact about
a mistyped URL, recorded as a fact about the site. FOUND BY FETCHING THE ISSUE
INDEX -- .../2004/fall/ -- AND READING ITS TABLE OF CONTENTS, which lists
"Traveling Out of the Comfort Zone" and, in the article's own sidebar,
"Traveling (Page 2)" at two/index.html.

=====================================================================
WHY IT MATTERS: THE MAN, NOT THE FACTS
=====================================================================

James Caddell (1973-2005) is one half of the Pip Alumni Award's memorial and a
Kanawana camper and counsellor from 1983. This project already knows his life
in detail, from his CMAT obituary and other second-hand accounts.

WHAT IT DID NOT HAVE IS HIM WRITING. This is a signed first-person dispatch,
published about a year before he died, describing the trip he died on. Beside
the Carol Skinner blog it is the second first-person long-form document by a
Kanawana person this project has identified, and unlike that one it is
readable.

=====================================================================
THE ONE LINE THAT TOUCHES CAMP -- AND WHAT IS NOT THERE
=====================================================================

  "Although we consider ourselves outdoorsy types, BEING VETERAN CANOE
  TRIPPERS, neither of us have much interest in hunting or fishing."

THAT IS ALL. KANAWANA IS NOT NAMED ANYWHERE IN EITHER PAGE. Neither is the
YMCA, nor summer camp, nor Quebec. Both pages were searched for all of them.
The phrase is worth having because the man who wrote it had been canoe
tripping at Kanawana since 1983 and because canoe tripping is what that camp
is for -- but the article does not make that connection and neither should
anyone quoting it.

=====================================================================
WHAT HE SAYS, IN HIS OWN WORDS
=====================================================================

THE OPENING, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POSTURE OF THE TRIP:

  "After a year and a half of saving every penny, purging our possessions,
  quitting our stable government jobs and leaving our comfortable Ottawa
  apartment, my wife Tara and I set off on a trip around the world. While our
  friends were starting families in their newly acquired four-bedroom houses,
  we were becoming hobos, left with nothing but what was in our backpacks. We
  wondered if we were totally insane, but we knew that a journey across six of
  the world's continents would provide us with an experience no university or
  employer could."

THEIR OWN ACCOUNT OF THEIR CAREERS, which differs slightly in wording from the
obituary this project has used:

  "We both received BAs from McGill in political science and history. McGill
  was good to us ... Tara was president of the Students' Society in 1997-98 and
  I was able to take a year off school in 1995 to serve a tour as a UN
  peacekeeper in Bosnia. These experiences, combined with a couple of MAs, led
  us to successful careers working for the federal government. I WAS A SENIOR
  ADVISOR IN THE CANADA STUDENT LOANS PROGRAM and TARA WAS THE MANAGER OF
  MINISTERIAL SUPPORT FOR THE NATIONAL SECRETARIAT ON HOMELESSNESS - both
  programs were part of Human Resources Development Canada."

  [The wiki, from the obituary, has him as "Senior Program Manager at Human
  Resources Development Canada". His own wording is narrower and names the
  programme. Not a conflict; a refinement from the man himself.]

WHERE THE IDEA CAME FROM -- A BROKEN RADIATOR CAP IN KENYA, ON THEIR HONEYMOON:

  "We started planning in the fall of 2002, roughly ten seconds after we
  returned from our honeymoon in Africa, where one small event profoundly
  affected us. While on our way to a national park in the north of Kenya, our
  Land Rover broke down in a tiny community of a few mud houses near the base
  of Mount Kenya. We'd been warned to avoid such impoverished communities for
  fear of being robbed. However, once stranded, we set out to explore ...
  The next few hours became the most memorable experience of our trip -
  hanging out with the local children who followed us around ... After a cap
  from an old water can was jerry-rigged with duct tape (MY SUGGESTION, SINCE
  ALL CANADIAN SOLDIERS LEARN THAT ANYTHING CAN BE FIXED WITH DUCT TAPE), the
  truck was ready ... Our happy accident made us realize that there were
  worlds outside of package tours that we wanted to explore."

THE BUDGET, WHICH THE OBITUARY ACCOUNTS DO NOT GIVE:

  "Our savings would allow us a budget of $100 CDN PER DAY in the U.S.,
  Australia and Western Europe, and $50 PER DAY in developing countries."

THE ITINERARY AS PLANNED: "North America, Australia, Southeast Asia, the
Indian subcontinent, the Middle East, Africa, Europe and South America."

THE DISTINCTION THE WHOLE PIECE TURNS ON:

  "our most important goal was to avoid exchanging one comfortable bubble for
  another - the tourist bubble. The tourist is comfortable on organized tours,
  eats familiar foods, and stays in approved hotels, while the traveler lives
  with locals, eats indigenous cuisine, and avoids the beaten path."

PAGE TWO is a set of headed lessons -- "Understand Local Geography and
Politics", "Always Put Your Hook in the Water", "Join an International Travel
Organization", "Throw Away the Guidebook", "Plug in Locally" -- with:

  * the shark. Sailing at Possum's Bay outside Hobart, Tasmania, with a
    skipper named SIMON FIRTH, Tara fishes for the first time and lands "a
    five-foot-long shark"; Firth takes them home to eat it with his wife, his
    brother and his ninety-year-old mother. (The article's photograph caption:
    "James with Simon Firth preparing the shark Tara caught for dinner, in
    Hobart, Tasmania.")
  * SERVAS, "a United Nations-affiliated travel organization" whose object is
    "to encourage peace through travel", through free home-stays. They name
    two hosts: Arie, a retired Dutch house painter outside Sydney, and John
    and Margaret in Darwin.
  * EAST TIMOR, two years after independence: "The capital of Dili was home to
    burned-out buildings, a destroyed infrastructure and people simply trying
    to survive day to day. We were moved and humbled by the sense of humour
    and inner strength of the people we met. After years of struggle and
    oppression the Timorese were not hardened, but were the warmest and
    kindest people we had encountered." A photograph caption: "James with
    Timorese children in Sananain, East Timor."
  * and the decision, in Dili, to stop being visitors: "we decided a better
    approach to understanding the culture would be to do volunteer work. We
    began networking with the UN and a few [NGOs]" -- which is the thread that
    runs on to the CMAT tsunami orphanage work in Tamil Nadu that the wiki
    already records.

The page footer reads "Page last updated: Mar. 3, 2006" -- four months after
his death.

=====================================================================
STILL NOT RECOVERED, AND NOW LOCATED
=====================================================================

THE CMAT OBITUARY (src_cmat_caddell_obituary, cmat.ca/james-caddell-soldier-
adventurer-1973-2005/) IS STILL 404 ON THE LIVE SITE -- confirmed today with a
browser user-agent, 404 with an 18 KB rebuilt-site page. But the Internet
Archive has exactly one capture of it:

    2 DECEMBER 2021, HTTP 200
    http://web.archive.org/web/20211202043604/https://cmat.ca/james-caddell-soldier-adventurer-1973-2005/

web.archive.org is unreachable from this environment (see f_5361), so this is
an operator task -- but a one-click one, and the record can stop saying the
obituary is lost.
